sections.summary: The neutral reading presents God's voice from the inner sanctuary commanding the seven angels to pour out the bowls of wrath; the section is a divine command initiating judgment rather than a statement about the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The First Bowl -- Sores on the Beast's Worshipers
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the first bowl producing sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped his image; the section narrates judgment on beast-worshipers rather than addressing the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Second Bowl -- The Sea Becomes Blood
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the second bowl turning the sea to blood, killing every living thing in it; the section narrates an Exodus-type plague rather than addressing the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Third Bowl -- Rivers Become Blood, and the Declaration of Divine Justice
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the third bowl turning rivers and springs to blood, with the angel of the waters and the altar declaring God's judgments righteous because the persecutors shed the saints' blood and now receive blood to drink; the section vindicates the martyrs rather than directly addressing the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Fourth Bowl -- Scorching Heat from the Sun
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the fourth bowl causing the sun to scorch people with fire; they blasphemed God and did not repent; the section describes the hardened response of beast-worshipers rather than addressing the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Fifth Bowl -- Darkness on the Beast's Throne
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the fifth bowl bringing darkness on the beast's kingdom; the afflicted blasphemed God and did not repent of their deeds; the section describes the hardened response of beast-worshipers rather than addressing the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Sixth Bowl -- The Euphrates Dried Up
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the sixth bowl drying up the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east; the section is a narrative of eschatological warfare preparation rather than a statement about the believer's standing.

The neutral reading describes three frog-like unclean spirits from the dragon, beast, and false prophet performing signs to gather the kings for the war of the great day of God; the section narrates demonic deception of world powers rather than addressing the believer's standing.

The neutral reading identifies this as a direct, parenthetical statement from the risen Christ to the assemblies, using the thief simile and pronouncing the third beatitude: blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes so as not to walk about naked in shame.
sections.relevance: This is a direct word from Christ to believers within the eschatological narrative, using the conditional beatitude form: blessedness depends on two ongoing actions -- staying awake (grēgorōn) and keeping one's clothes (tērōn ta himatia). The neutral reading connects both verbs to the letters: the Sardis warning to 'wake up' (3:2-3), the Laodicean nakedness of spiritual complacency (3:17-18), and the Sardis commendation of those who 'have not soiled their garments' (3:4). The neutral reading explicitly states that garments 'represent covenant faithfulness, moral integrity, and the identity of one who belongs to the Lamb' and that keeping one's clothes means 'to maintain one's covenant standing -- to remain faithful.' The conditional structure of the beatitude -- blessed is the one who maintains vigilance and covenant fidelity -- directly implies that standing before God requires ongoing maintenance, not merely initial reception.
key_phrases: Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes
so that he will not walk about naked and men will not see his shame
I am coming like a thief

sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the gathering of the kings at Har-Magedon, a name evoking the Jezreel Valley battle traditions from Israel's history; the section is a geographical-eschatological reference rather than a statement about the believer's standing.
